title: Erdős Problem #238: Consecutive Primes with Large Gaps
description: For c₁, c₂ > 0, can we find > c₁·log(x) consecutive primes ≤ x with all gaps > c₂? Proved for small c₁ (Erdős); general case OPEN.

overview.historicalContext:
This problem from Erdős [Er55c, p.7; Er49c] concerns long runs of consecutive primes with uniformly large gaps. The Prime Number Theorem ensures average gaps grow as log(x), so most gaps exceed any fixed constant for large x. The challenge is finding LONG runs where ALL gaps are large.

Erdős proved the conjecture holds when c₁ is sufficiently small (depending on c₂). The general case — arbitrary c₁, c₂ > 0 — remains open. Cramér's conjecture on maximal gaps provides supporting context.
overview.problemStatement: Let c₁, c₂ > 0. Is it true that for any sufficiently large x, there exist more than c₁·log(x) consecutive primes ≤ x such that the difference between any two adjacent primes is > c₂?
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines nthPrime, primeGap, consecutivePrimes, and predicates allPrimesLeX and allGapsLarge. The main conjecture uses Filter.Eventually (∀ᶠ in atTop). Erdős's partial result is an axiom. PNT context, run length analysis, and Cramér's conjecture are included. A summary theorem combines the known results.
keyInsights: Average prime gap near x is ~log(x) by PNT, so most gaps exceed any fixed c₂
The challenge is finding LONG runs (length c₁·log x) where ALL gaps are large
Erdős proved the result for sufficiently small c₁ (depending on c₂)
The general case (arbitrary c₁ > 0) remains open
Cramér's conjecture on maximal gaps provides supporting context

sections.summary: consecutivePrimes (k primes starting from p_m), allPrimesLeX (bounded by x), allGapsLarge (all k-1 gaps exceed c₂)

sections.title: Part 3: The Main Conjecture
sections.summary: mainConjecture: ∀ c₁, c₂ > 0, ∀ᶠ x in atTop, ∃ run of k > c₁·log(x) primes ≤ x with all gaps > c₂

sections.title: Part 4: The Negation
sections.summary: conjectureNegation: what failure means — ∃ c₁, c₂ blocking long large-gap runs for infinitely many x

sections.title: Part 5: Erdős's Partial Result
sections.summary: erdos_partial_result (axiom): ∀ c₂ > 0, ∃ c₁ > 0 (small, depending on c₂) making the conjecture hold. The ∃c₁ vs ∀c₁ quantifier swap is the open gap.

sections.title: Part 6: PNT Context
sections.summary: average_gap_grows (axiom): some gap near x exceeds c₂. prime_number_theorem_asymptotic (axiom): π(x) ~ x/log(x)

sections.title: Part 7: Run Length Analysis
sections.summary: maxRunLength via sSup and conjecture_implies_run_growth (axiom): conjecture ⟹ run length grows as log(x)

sections.title: Part 8: Heuristic Analysis
sections.summary: large_gaps_eventually_dominate (PROVED theorem): for fixed c₂, some gap near x exceeds c₂. Proved by forwarding to average_gap_grows.

sections.title: Part 9: Cramér's Conjecture
sections.summary: cramersConjecture definition: maximal prime gap ≤ C·(log x)². Open conjecture providing supporting context.

sections.title: Part 10: Structural Theorems and Summary
sections.summary: partial_weaker_than_full (PROVED): full conjecture ⟹ partial. conjecture_vs_negation (PROVED): full ⟹ ¬negation. erdos_238_summary: combines partial result.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #238 asks whether long runs of consecutive primes with all gaps > c₂ can always be found. Erdős proved this for small c₁; the general case remains open.
conclusion.implications: Resolution would illuminate prime gap distribution and whether gaps exhibit sufficient uniformity to support long runs of large values.
openQuestions: Does the conjecture hold for all c₁, c₂ > 0?
What is the optimal dependence of c₁ on c₂ in Erdős's partial result?
How does the answer relate to Cramér's conjecture on maximal gaps?
Can probabilistic models (Cramér random model) be made rigorous for this problem?

crossReferences.description: Maynard-Tao bounded gaps prove infinitely many gaps ≤ 246; Problem #238 asks about long runs where ALL gaps are large — opposite end of the gap distribution spectrum
The PNT (π(x) ~ x/log x) establishes that average prime gap near x is ~log x, which is the fundamental reason large gaps become common for large x
Both concern collective properties of consecutive primes: #17 asks about differences covering all even numbers (cluster primes), #238 asks about long runs with all gaps large
